records.prompt:
Consider the following functions, defined for all real \(x\):
\[
f_1(x)=x,\qquad f_2(x)=x\cos x,\qquad f_3(x)=3e^{2x},\qquad f_4(x)=x-|x|.
\]
Answer parts (a)–(d) about each function by writing Yes or No in the response grid. No justification is required in the historical question; every blank is scored as incorrect.

partsPatches.prompt: Does \(f(-x)=-f(x)\)? Give four answers in the order \(f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4\).
partsPatches.answer: \(f_1:\text{ Yes},\ f_2:\text{ Yes},\ f_3:\text{ No},\ f_4:\text{ No}.\) Indeed, \(f_1\) is odd and \(f_2(-x)=(-x)\cos(-x)=-x\cos x=-f_2(x)\). The exponential is not odd. Also, \(f_4(x)=2x\) for \(x<0\) and \(f_4(x)=0\) for \(x\ge0\), so it is not odd.

partsPatches.prompt: Does the inverse function exist for all \(x\)?
partsPatches.answer: \(f_1:\text{ Yes},\ f_2:\text{ No},\ f_3:\text{ Yes},\ f_4:\text{ No}.\) The identity and \(3e^{2x}\) are one-to-one. The function \(x\cos x\) is not one-to-one, and \(x-|x|=0\) for every \(x\ge0\).
No for all four functions. A continuous periodic function on \(\mathbb R\) is bounded, whereas each of these four functions is unbounded on at least one side of its domain.

Yes for all four functions. The first three are compositions and products of continuous functions. For \(f_4\), the left-hand formula is \(2x\), the right-hand formula is \(0\), and both one-sided limits equal \(f_4(0)=0\).

records.facsimileAuthority: The historical question-region SVG and full source-page SVG for PDF page 3 are authoritative for the four functions, the Yes/No row wording, and the rectangular response-grid format.
records.workedSolution:
**(a) Oddness.** \(f_1\) is odd. Since cosine is even, \(f_2(-x)=(-x)\cos(-x)=-x\cos x=-f_2(x)\), so \(f_2\) is odd. For \(f_3\), \(f_3(-x)=3e^{-2x}\ne-3e^{2x}\), so the answer is No. For \(f_4\), writing it piecewise gives \(f_4(x)=2x\) for \(x<0\) and \(0\) for \(x\ge0\); it is not odd. Thus: **Yes, Yes, No, No**.

**(b) Inverses.** \(f_1\) is one-to-one. The function \(f_2=x\cos x\) repeats output values (for example, it has infinitely many zeros), so it is not one-to-one. \(f_3=3e^{2x}\) is strictly increasing and therefore invertible on \(\mathbb R\). \(f_4\) is constant on \([0,\infty)\), so it is not one-to-one. Thus: **Yes, No, Yes, No**.

**(c) Periodicity.** All four answers are No. In particular, \(x\cos x\) is not periodic merely because \(\cos x\) is periodic: its amplitude grows with \(|x|\). More generally, all four functions are unbounded on at least one side, whereas a continuous periodic function on \(\mathbb R\) is bounded.

**(d) Continuity at the origin.** The identity, product \(x\cos x\), and exponential are continuous. For \(f_4\), \(\lim_{x\to0^-}2x=0=\lim_{x\to0^+}0=f_4(0)\). Thus: **Yes, Yes, Yes, Yes**.
records.alternativeSolution: Build a four-column property table. Use symmetry rules (odd times even is odd), monotonicity for inverse existence, boundedness as a quick necessary condition for continuous periodicity, and the piecewise form \(x-|x|=2x\) for \(x<0\), \(0\) for \(x\ge0\).

records.workedSolution:
Differentiate the position:
\[
v(t)=x'(t)=12t^3-48t^2+48t=12t(t-2)^2.
\]
Differentiate once more:
\[
a(t)=v'(t)=36t^2-96t+48=12(3t-2)(t-2).
\]
The particle is at rest where \(v(t)=0\), namely \(t=0\) and \(t=2\). Because \((t-2)^2\ge0\), the sign of \(v(t)\) away from its zeros is the sign of \(t\). Thus velocity changes from negative to positive at \(t=0\), but it does not change sign at the double root \(t=2\). The only direction change is at \(t=0\).

Finally, \(a(t)=0\) at \(t=\frac23\) and \(t=2\). The first such time is \(t=\frac23\), and
\[
v\!\left(\frac23\right)=12\left(\frac23\right)\left(\frac23-2\right)^2=\frac{128}{9}.
\]
records.alternativeSolution: After differentiating, use a sign chart for \(v(t)=12t(t-2)^2\). The odd-multiplicity zero at \(0\) changes sign; the even-multiplicity zero at \(2\) does not.
